chapter: Teaching, the 1951 Big Show and New York nights
title: Life on the Big Show: Shorty Baker, Willie Smith's superstition, Cat Anderson
summary: Players kept disappearing at hometown stops, and Willie Smith always waited to be last on the bandstand.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: Yeah, '51. But any way, this is -- this was a great band, it was a great show, and as I said I could hardly wait to get to work every night because it was fireworks. Of course somebody was missing out of the band every night, you know, we'd leave -- we would leave Shorty Baker in St. Louis. I think his home was in St. Louis. If we passed through another town, another one would disappear. Willie Smith always got on the bandstand last. I think he was superstitious. He would wait until everyone had got on
that -- had got on the bandstand, then he would get on. It was a superstition. He was a very superstitious man, you know.
I knew Willie but I wasn't aware he was superstitious.
I never knew about his superstitions, but I've since heard about them
He would never get on -- it was a thing with him. He would stand over on the side until everybody got on, then he would --
That's right. I'm telling you it might be days. But we did -- and Cat Anderson was in the band, as you know. This was a -- I don't think Cootie was there this time.
No, Cootie wasn't back then, wasn't back then
